## Destination

The spec, where `authoring` places each part, with the scripts beside the skills that name
them, generalized from libgit2's names (`libgit2_tests`, `util_tests`, the
`LIBGIT2_RUST_LIBRARY` variable, the `offline` and `util` targets) into arguments:

- `setup`, Builds, and `testing-builds`, Builds: the variants are built in generations, each
  from a worktree of the fork of its own, and a checkout's `crustify/builds` links to one; a
  switch builds the next generation, and the assistant moves the base checkout to it once
  the switch lands, so that the batches in flight keep theirs. `build-variants.sh` beside
  `setup`.
- `bindgen`, Build modes: the `staticlib` form of campaign mode, and that campaign mode leaves
  the library the C links out of its own links.
- `testing-builds`, Builds: each variant's C consumers link a library built with its
  instrumentation, by `rust-staticlib.sh`, including BSan's form above.
- `testing-gates`, Regressions: a switch's C tests run by `c-tests.sh` per variant the
  baseline records, compared with it.
- `porting-workflow`, Builds: the order a switch's steps take, the C build's `configure`
  before the Rust library and its link after it.
- `porting-workflow`, One language per module (item 6): an equivalence test that calls no C
  is carried over to the module's unit tests at the switch, not retired with the file.
- `testing-gates`, Regressions (item 5): a link unit that no C test reaches is checked at its
  switch by its relinked executables beside the previous generation's, by a tracked script
  beside `c-tests.sh`, and the result compared with the module pass's record.
- `reviewing` (item 7): whether a switch updates the reproducers that name its export
  feature.
- `build-variants.sh` (item 8): a job count, divided among the variants it builds.
- `bindgen`, Build modes, or the fork's `SelectRust.cmake` (item 9): the C library's link
  collects the Rust it does not call.
- `porting-workflow`, Builds (item 10): the switch's Rust side, the bindings regenerated,
  lands before the generation is built, since every variant's build checks them.
- `testing-gates`, Regressions (item 11): a switch whose exports only the baseline's disabled
  online suites reach runs those the target's own CI runs against local servers, against a
  local remote, by the scripts beside `c-tests.sh`, on the new generation and the previous
  one, compared; `http-remote.py` and `http-gate.sh` generalized from libgit2's suites and
  variables into arguments.
- `porting-workflow`, One language per module (item 12): the carry-over candidates are the
  retiring tests without the Miri `calls C` marker.
- The `libgit2` CMake lesson (item 13): a property naming the removed file is left.
- `porting-workflow`, Builds (item 14): deleting the export feature removes every mention of
  its name in the crate, not only the gateway's `cfg`.
- `testing-gates`, Regressions (item 15): a switch checks its archive by the symbols the
  removed TU defined, or by object path, not by member names.
- `http-gate.sh` (item 16): connections are tallied beside requests, so that a keep-alive
  departure shows.
- `setup`, Builds, or `build.json` (item 17): the variants' smoke test is named once, from
  C that stays.

## Change

Made in the campaign only: the scripts under `crustify/scripts/`, `build.rs`'s campaign
mode and `build.json` version 7, and, from `deps/llhttp/api.c`'s switch, `http-remote.py`
and `http-gate.sh` beside `c-tests.sh`. The skills are not changed by this run: the change spans
`setup`, `bindgen`, `testing-builds` and `testing-gates`, which are not the translator's to
evolve, and wants its own review.

## Validation

This run: `build-variants.sh` built the five variants of `crustify/builds.gen1` from the
fork's `1b37e3d08`, each smoke-tested (`util_tests -sutf8`); the workspace's gates ran over
them and `c-tests.sh` compared four variants with the baseline, as the dashboard entry
records. A later switch validates the generalized scripts by running them.

`src/cli/opt.c`'s switch ran `build-variants.sh`, `rust-staticlib.sh` and `c-tests.sh`
unchanged, for a second link unit, and its gates over `crustify/builds.gen2` are its
dashboard entry's. Items 5 to 9 are its evidence, and are not made: `porting-workflow` is the
translator's to evolve, but item 6 wants review with the rest of this proposal.

`deps/llhttp/api.c`'s switch ran the three scripts unchanged again, for a third module, the
first whose exports libgit2 itself calls only over the network. Its gates over
`crustify/builds.gen3` are its dashboard entry's. Item 11's two scripts are made, in the
campaign only (`crustify/scripts/http-remote.py` and `http-gate.sh`), and validated by that
run: gen2's C and gen3's Rust give the same `results.txt` on plain, ASan+UBSan and TSan, and on
gen3's coverage variant the run calls 24 of the 31 exports. A mutant of an export was not
built, so whether the comparison catches a departure rests on the coverage alone. Items 10,
12 and 13 are evidence, and are not made: they want review with the rest of this proposal.

`deps/llhttp/http.c`'s switch ran the scripts again, for a fourth module, and changed one:
item 16's connection tally, in `http-remote.py`'s log and `http-gate.sh`'s `results.txt`, in
the campaign only, validated by four identical runs over gen4 and gen5's equal ones. Items 14,
15 and 17 are evidence, and are not made.

## Review

content.content:
# Map of `module-switch-procedure`'s 17 items

Source: `crustify/evolution/module-switch-procedure/PROPOSAL.md`. Drafts:
`crustify/tmp/assistant/split/<slug>/PROPOSAL.md` and `LESSONS-draft.md`.

| item | what it is | taken by | kind |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | the variants cannot be rebuilt in place | `variant-generations` | proposal |
| 2 | campaign mode cannot build the Rust library the C links | `rust-library-per-variant` | proposal |
| 3 | BorrowSanitizer has no `rustc` subcommand | `rust-library-per-variant` | proposal |
| 4 | the C test gate was scratch | `switch-c-tests-baseline` | proposal |
| 5 | a link unit no C test reaches | `switch-gate-beyond-c-tests` | proposal |
| 6 | equivalence tests that run no C are lost | `equiv-tests-without-c` | proposal |
| 7 | a reproducer names the deleted export feature | `reproducers-of-deleted-feature` | proposal |
| 8 | `build-variants.sh` takes no job count | `variant-generations` | proposal |
| 9 | the C library's link pulls Rust it never calls | `c-link-unused-rust` | proposal |
| 10 | the switch's Rust side precedes the generation | `switch-step-order` (whole); one sentence repeated in `variant-generations` and `rust-library-per-variant` | proposal |
| 11 | a module only an online suite reaches | `switch-gate-beyond-c-tests` (the rule); `http-exports-gated-through-a-local-remote` (libgit2's facts) | proposal and lesson |
| 12 | the tests that call no C are marked already | `equiv-tests-without-c` | proposal |
| 13 | a CMake file names the removed source in a property | `cmake-property-naming-a-removed-source` | lesson |
| 14 | the export feature is named outside the gateway's `cfg` | `switch-step-order` | proposal |
| 15 | an archive's member names are not unique | `switch-archive-check` | proposal |
| 16 | the HTTP gate did not see keep-alive | `http-gate-tallies-connections` | lesson |
| 17 | the variants' smoke test is gone | `variant-generations` | proposal |

Nine proposals and three lessons.

## Where the grouping departs from the suggested one

- Item 9 is a proposal of its own, not with items 2 and 3. Items 2 and 3 are made in the
  campaign and ran at four switches. Item 9 is "not tried", has two candidate fixes, and one
  of its destinations is the fork's own CMake file. It can be reviewed, or declined, alone.
- Items 4, 5 with 11, and 15 are three proposals, not one. Item 4 moves one script
  (`c-tests.sh`). Items 5 and 11 are one rule (exports no baseline C test reaches) with
  other scripts. Item 15 changes a check and moves no script.
- Item 10 is not split. `switch-step-order` takes it whole. Its sentences on the generation
  (each variant's build checks the committed bindings; the bindings are regenerated against
  the previous generation) are repeated in `variant-generations`' Evidence with a pointer.

## Text of the original placed in more than one draft

- The "Items 1 to 4" bullets of the second, third and fourth switches mix facts of several
  items. Each sentence is copied to every draft it bears on: build times and object counts
  to `variant-generations`; object counts and the symbols each link unit defines to
  `switch-archive-check`; the symbols and the CLI's link to `rust-library-per-variant`;
  "`c-tests.sh` ran unchanged" to `switch-c-tests-baseline`; the 907 dynamic symbols and
  6747 Rust functions to `c-link-unused-rust`; the smoke tests to `variant-generations`.
- Validation's first paragraph (gen1) is copied to `variant-generations`,
  `rust-library-per-variant` and `switch-c-tests-baseline`.
- Item 11's evidence is copied to the proposal and to the lesson.

## Text of the original placed by judgement

- Destination, "`porting-workflow`, Builds: the order a switch's steps take, the C build's
  `configure` before the Rust library and its link after it". It carries no item number and
  follows from item 2. It is placed in `switch-step-order`, with item 2's sentence on where
  `rust-staticlib.sh` runs copied there.
- Destination, "The `libgit2` CMake lesson (item 13): a property naming the removed file is
  left". The draft is a new entry that points at the existing lesson. It could instead be an
  edit of that entry, which would make that entry `provisional` again.
- Evidence, the second switch's sentences on the CLI's link unit (`SelectRust.cmake`, the
  crate's default features). They hold for libgit2 alone. They are kept as evidence in
  `rust-library-per-variant`, and are neither a rule there nor a lesson.
- Evidence, item 1: "The side campaigns' installs, reached as `$PWD/../../../..`, resolve the
  same from a sibling of `builds`." Kept in `variant-generations`; the rule it implies (a
  generation sits at the same depth as the shared builds) is not written into the Change.

## Text of the original not placed

- The Signal's opening sentence, "Procedures worked out by hand that the skills should
  state, …, and two gaps where following the skills as written fails". No row of the
  Signals table reads "a procedure worked out by hand that a skill should state". Each
  draft names the nearest row; `c-link-unused-rust` and `reproducers-of-deleted-feature` say
  that no row fits exactly.
- The Change section's reason: "the change spans `setup`, `bindgen`, `testing-builds` and
  `testing-gates`, which are not the translator's to evolve, and wants its own review". Each
  draft lists its protected paths instead. `setup` and `bindgen` are not on the protected
  list given for this split, though the original calls them not the translator's.
- Validation, "`porting-workflow` is the translator's to evolve, but item 6 wants review
  with the rest of this proposal", and "they want review with the rest of this proposal"
  (items 10, 12, 13). Copied where the items went, but "the rest of this proposal" no longer
  exists once the split is filed. `equiv-tests-without-c` and `switch-step-order` touch only
  `porting-workflow`, which is not protected.
- The first switch's note in the Destination preamble that the scripts sit "beside the
  skills that name them". It does not say which skill `rust-staticlib.sh` sits beside.
- "Review: Pending." and "Status: `open`." of the original, and its row in
  `crustify/evolution/INDEX.md` (runs `wave-186/batch-7`, `wave-194/batch-7`). The split
  needs the original marked `superseded` by the nine slugs and nine index rows; not done.

## Gaps noticed while splitting

- The original never records how gen4 was built. Evidence names gen1, gen2, gen3 and gen5,
  and uses gen4 only as the previous generation of the fourth switch.
- The evolution skill's Proposals section asks each proposal for "the row the record takes
  when the change lands". The section list given for these drafts has no Record section, so
  none is written. Each draft needs one before it lands.
- `http-gate-tallies-connections` holds a general idea in libgit2's names: a comparison gate
  shows a departure only if its lines depend on what each export returns. If a second gate

# The packaging gate's procedure, for a crate whose dependencies are unpublished

Status: `open`.

## Signal

A procedure worked out by hand that a skill should state: `testing-gates`' Regressions
section says that a batch that changes the raw bindings packages the safe crate, "built
alone in bundled mode from the C it packages, with no build variant selected", and that
"each crate the package depends on is patched to its local source", but not how. The
direct form fails, and the steps that pass were found by trial.

## Evidence

`wave-229/batch-0/run-1` (`src/util/utf8.c`, which allowlists three functions), on base
`2216b0cd0`, the first packaging gate since the tree's change of 2026-11-13:

1. `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT= cargo package --offline --allow-dirty` stops before verifying:
   `no matching package named glibc-bindings found` (crates.io index). The packaged
   manifest drops the Git source of `glibc-bindings` and the path of `ffibox`, keeping
   their versions, and the workspace's `[patch]` tables, keyed by those sources, do not
   apply to it.
2. `cargo package --offline --allow-dirty --no-verify --exclude-lockfile` packages (697
   files). Extracted under `crustify/tmp/`, the package's manifest needs an empty
   `[workspace]`, since the worktree's own encloses it, and
   `[patch.crates-io] glibc-bindings = { path = "/target/glibc-crustify" }` and
   `ffibox = { path = "/crustify-rs/ffibox" }`.
3. `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT= cargo build --offline` there then fails in CMake: PCRE2, then
   zlib, not found. The host has neither: the bundled build finds them only through the
   side campaigns' `plain` installs, `OPENSSL_ROOT_DIR` and `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH`, the
   latter `:`-separated in the environment where `build.json`'s `-D` form takes `;`.

   builds alone: cmake builds `libgit2.a` and `libcrustify_git2.a` into `OUT_DIR`.

`f68ea8660`), the next packaging gate, followed steps 2 and 3 and failed to compile the
package's `lib`: two copies of ffibox, `0.1.1` by path for the crate and `0.1.0` by Git
(`40621a2`) for `glibc-bindings`, whose manifest takes ffibox by Git. The workspace patches
that Git source too (`[patch."https://github.com/crustify-rs/ffibox"]`), and step 2's
`[patch.crates-io]` does not stand for it. `opt.rs`'s gateway, which compiles from this switch
on, is the first code of the crate to pass a `glibc_bindings` `FileRef` through the crate's
own ffibox traits (`FileRef::from_ptr`, E0599 four times), so `utf8.c`'s gate could not have
met it. With the workspace's Git patch copied into the package's manifest as well, and the
lockfile the first attempt wrote removed, so that the patch applies, the graph holds one
ffibox and the package builds alone (696 files). Its `lib` tests: 829 pass and 58 fail, the
58 needing `c/tests/resources`, as at `utf8.c`'s gate. So the script copies every `[patch]`
table of the workspace, the Git sources' as well as crates.io's, and resolves with no
lockfile.

`wave-219/batch-0/run-1` (`src/util/cc-compat.h`, which allowlists three constants), an
occurrence, on base `f7f0eaaa0`: step 2 packaged 696 files. In the extracted package, the
manifest took an empty `[workspace]`, the `[patch.crates-io]` entries of step 2 and both of the
workspace's Git `[patch]` tables, and no lockfile. Then step 3's `cargo build --offline`, with
no variant and the side installs on `OPENSSL_ROOT_DIR`, `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH` and
`PKG_CONFIG_PATH`, built the package alone: cmake built `libgit2.a` and `libcrustify_git2.a`
into `OUT_DIR`. The batch worked the procedure out again from this proposal's evidence.

## Destination

The spec: `testing-gates`' Regressions section, with a script beside it, as `authoring`
places a procedure that must run exactly so, documented by its `--help`: it packages
without verifying, patches each unpublished dependency to the source the workspace's
`[patch]` names for it, gives the extracted package a workspace of its own, puts the
out-of-tree libraries' installs of the `plain` variant on the build system's search paths,
and builds it with no variant, in a scratch dir it removes.

## Change

Not made: the gate is not a translator's to change. The section would name the script,
and say that the patches and search paths stand in for what a dependent's host supplies.

verified the tree of `wave-186/batch-0`, after two forms that failed:

```bash
S=$(realpath -m crustify/builds/plain/../../../..)
I() { echo "$S/$1-bindings/crustify/builds/plain/install"; }
CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT= OPENSSL_ROOT_DIR=$(I openssl) \
CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="$(I openssl):$(I pcre2):$(I zlib)" \
PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$(I pcre2)/lib/pkgconfig:$(I zlib)/lib/pkgconfig" \
cargo package --allow-dirty \
  --config 'patch.crates-io.glibc-bindings.path="/target/glibc-crustify"' \
  --config 'patch.crates-io.ffibox.path="/crustify-rs/ffibox"'
```

The run above, step by step: step 1 fails as quoted, steps 2 and 3 pass. A script is
validated by passing on that tree and failing, naming the library, without the search
paths.

Fill in as many answers as you want before starting Crustify. It will ask only
for campaign decisions that remain unresolved.

# Mandatory questions

## Campaign

1. **Which repository and revision should this campaign use?** (`id: source`)
   - Answer: `https://github.com/libgit2/libgit2.git`, `0551dfd4a` (the `c/` submodule):
     the revision of the checkout at `/target` the campaign started from

2. **Should this campaign port the C implementation to Rust, or create safe
   Rust wrappers?** (`id: campaign`)
   - Answer: `port`

3. **What should this campaign target: a named subset of modules, or a named
   subset of functions and types, or the whole target repo? You can define them
   now or we can brainstorm them during the live session. You can also let the
   assistant decide.** (`id: scope`)
   - Answer: the whole target, excluding deprecated items, building up on the
     previous wrap campaign.

4. **Which agent CLI and billing should do the translation work?**
   (`id: translate-agent`)
   - Answer: `claude, api, proxy: openrouter, args: --model claude-opus-5-5`

5. **Do you want agentic review after translated work lands? If so, which
   agent CLI and billing should perform each review?** (`id: review-agent`)
   - Answer: `claude, api, proxy: openrouter, args: --model claude-opus-5-5`, after each wave

6. **Should I run fully autonomously end to end?** (`id: autonomy`)
   - Answer: `no`

# Optional questions

Unanswered optional questions use their defaults.

## Campaign execution

7. **Which agent CLI and billing should plan the campaign, and how many planner runs
   should it make? Each run emits what the plan lacks and corrects what the runs
   before it committed.** (`id: plan-agent`)
   - Answer: `claude, api, proxy: openrouter, args: --model claude-opus-5-5, runs: 2`

8. **Should batches and parallelism be capped? Each wave's batches are packed when it
   starts, sized by its items, the agents and the host; a cap bounds every batch, or the
   agents running at once.** (`id: workload`)
   - Answer: `assistant's choice`

9. **Should review batches be capped? They are packed larger than translation batches,
   since a reviewer reads landed code rather than writing it.** (`id: review-workload`)
   - Answer: `assistant's choice`

10. **Which objectives should review agents review for? By default, every one the
    reviewer offers.** (`id: review-objectives`)
    - Answer: `all`
    - Without `fix`, reviewers report and reproduce what they find but patch nothing.

11. **Which sanitizers should the campaign build and test under? By default, every one
    the toolchain supports.** (`id: sanitizers`)
    - Answer: `asan-ubsan, tsan, bsan`, the variants `crustify/artifacts/build.json`
      records; MSan is not built.
    - From 2026-11-14 BSan runs as the `testing-gates` skill's Regressions section has it,
      with no departure: for a batch, on the tests its own work adds or changes, each named
      and alone; at a wave's and a module's end, over the workspace less the slow list,
      `crustify/scripts/slow-list.txt`; and whole in each full run. The departure of
      2026-11-13, BSan over the workspace only before a ship point, ended when that rule
      landed.
    - Miri needs no build and is always on.

12. **How should the target be configured: which of its build features should be
    enabled or disabled?** (`id: target-config`)
    - Answer: the configuration `crustify/artifacts/build.json` records: deprecated
      features disabled (`-DDEPRECATE_HARD=ON`), HTTPS through OpenSSL, SSH, Negotiate
      auth and i18n off, threads on.

13. **At which points should the hybrid C-Rust program ship? Shipping advances `main` to
    what the campaign has integrated, with your approval each time: the modules shipped
    are translated, and the C still left is reached only through the wrappers on its
    boundary.** (`id: ship`)
    - Answer: `after:` `src/libgit2/repository.c` and every module its `schedule.json`
      record reaches through `depends_on.scheduled`, 42 modules of about 15.8K lines of C,
      their `wrap` and `port` waves planned through wave 781: `src/libgit2/buf.c`,
      `src/libgit2/common.h`, `src/libgit2/config.c`, `src/libgit2/grafts.c`,
      `src/libgit2/object.c`, `src/libgit2/odb.c`, `src/libgit2/oid.c`,
      `src/libgit2/oidarray.c`, `src/libgit2/parse.c`, `src/libgit2/refs.c`,
      `src/libgit2/repository.c`, `src/libgit2/strarray.c`, `src/libgit2/sysdir.c`,
      `src/util/alloc.c`, `src/util/allocators/failalloc.c`, `src/util/array.h`,
      `src/util/cc-compat.h`, `src/util/ctype_compat.h`, `src/util/errors.c`,
      `src/util/filebuf.c`, `src/util/fs_path.c`, `src/util/futils.c`, `src/util/hash.c`,
      `src/util/hash/collisiondetect.c`, `src/util/hash/openssl.c`,
      `src/util/hash/sha1dc/sha1.c`, `src/util/hash/sha1dc/ubc_check.c`,
      `src/util/hashmap.h`, `src/util/hashmap_str.h`, `src/util/integer.h`,
      `src/util/pool.c`, `src/util/posix.c`, `src/util/rand.c`, `src/util/regexp.c`,
      `src/util/runtime.c`, `src/util/str.c`, `src/util/thread.c`, `src/util/tsort.c`,
      `src/util/unix/map.c`, `src/util/unix/realpath.c`, `src/util/util.c`,
      `src/util/vector.c`: the first ship point, chosen by the user on 2026-11-15 in place
      of the list by size (about 15K lines of integrated leaves, through wave 338). A
      re-plan that changes the closure changes this list with it. `src/util/alloc.c` and
      `src/util/allocators/failalloc.c` are wrapped, not ported, and the dependencies the
      order cuts stay C behind wrappers at this point. Later points are core modules
      with their closures too, each confirmed with the user; `src/libgit2/commit.c`, nine
      modules further, is the candidate for the second.
    - `decide after planning`: once the plan is complete, I propose ship points from it,
      with the boundary each would leave, and record your choice here.
    - By default: after every integrated module.

## Evolution

14. **How far may the campaign evolve Crustify and its tools from what it exposes? Agents
    file proposals and record the target's lessons; fixes and improvements land, once
    another agent has reviewed them, on a working branch of each component that is the
    campaign's own, and reach the component's `devel` only with your approval.**
    (`id: evolution`)
    - Answer: `evolve`, on the campaign's working branches (`libgit2-crustify/devel` of each
      component, checked out since 2026-11-14 in a worktree of its own beside the
      component's checkout, `/crustify-rs/<component>.libgit2-crustify`, the component's
      own checkout being on `devel`; a session of this campaign loads Crustify from that
      worktree, `--plugin-dir /crustify-rs/crustify.libgit2-crustify`): a change lands
      there once its review approves it, and each component's `devel` takes the working
      branch only with the user's approval, as crustify `c2f21a0`'s model has it. The
      former `unattended: the whole campaign` is retired with it.
    - `propose`: proposals and lessons only. `repair`: also fixes of defects. `evolve`: also
      improvements and new tools. You are asked to take the working branches into `devel`
      at each module's end and the campaign's end.

## Commits

15. **Which git identity should the campaign's commits carry: an author, and any
    co-authors? By default, Crustify's own, `crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>` (the
    GitHub account `crustify-ai`), as the author, with no co-author.** (`id: identity`)
    - Answer: `author: Marius Momeu <marius.momeu@berkeley.edu>, co-authors: crustify
      <crustify@berkeley.edu>` (the GitHub account `crustify-ai`)

## Autonomy (if question 6 is answered `no`)

Answer these approval-gate questions only if question 6 is answered `no`.

16. **Should I wait for your approval before starting the setup phase?** (`id: gates.setup`)
    - Answer: `no`
17. **Should I wait for your approval before starting the translation phase?**
    (`id: gates.translation`)
    - Answer: `no`
18. **Should I wait for your approval before integrating each module into the working
    branch?** (`id: gates.module`)

name: versioning
description: "Repositories, branches, worktrees, landing under the landing lock, promotion, integration, their lifecycle, and the identity every commit takes. Read before the first commit, and before creating, landing on, promoting or purging any branch or worktree."

# Versioning

How a campaign's work is held in version control: the repositories it works in, their
branches and worktrees, how a batch lands its work and how each part is promoted. Where
things sit in the tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Repositories

A translation campaign produces a Rust codebase, so its repository is one: a new
repository created for the campaign, with the Rust at its root and the C it translates
inside it.

| campaign | repository | the C, under `c/` |
|---|---|---|
| wrap | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the source, pinned at the campaign's revision, which the campaign never changes |
| port | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the campaign's fork of the source, `<repo>-fork`, on its `main` branch, which the modules' switches trim as they leave C |

`<repo>` is the source repository's name: a campaign on libgit2 is `libgit2-crustify`,
and a port's fork `libgit2-fork`. A wrap and a port campaign share the name, since wrapping a
codebase is a step towards replacing its implementation: a port continues a wrap campaign
in its repository. Both keep the C's history where it belongs, so that it can be read in the
submodule and an upstream release taken in by rebasing the fork's `main` onto it. The fork
mirrors the source's own `main` as `upstream/main`. The repositories are created under the
`crustify-rs` organization; the campaign's tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

A library the target uses from outside its tree is wrapped in a wrap campaign of its own,
in `<source>-crustify`, named after the source it is built from, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md) describes.

An audit reviews an existing Rust crate in its own repository, and creates none.

## 2. Branches

| branch | name | checked out |
|---|---|---|
### 4.2 Commits

Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.

The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
describes.
<!-- TODO: when the working and shipping branches, and a wrapper's, are pushed to their
remotes is not specified yet, though a wrapper's reuse and a Git-pinned dependency need
it. -->

### 4.3 Promotion

A wave that has landed every batch is promoted to the branch it forked from, the module's
branch or the working branch, by a fast-forward to its tip, with the same local push
through the Git common directory, which rejects anything but a fast-forward.

### 4.4 Progress

The progress recorded while waves run, in `schedule.json`, the dashboard's usage and
campaign cells, and the `status` of a module in `modules.json` that a wrap batch ahead of
its consumer freezes, is committed on the working branch whenever no module is integrating. No agent writes
`schedule.json`, and no module branch changes it.

### 4.5 Integration

A module's branch is integrated into the working branch once the
last wave of its run has been promoted to it. Other modules may have been integrated since
it forked, so the working branch is merged into it, in its worktree, rather than the
other way around: the module's commits keep their ids, which its batches' `commits`
record, and the working branch still moves only by fast-forward.

1. The working branch's tip is merged into the module's branch. The files every module
   adds to, the dashboard's rows, the raw bindings' allowlists, `src/lib.rs`'s module
   declarations and the safe crate's export features, conflict additively, and so does a
   module's file in which two runs homed different items ahead of their consumers, with
   the declarations of the modules on its path: each conflict
   keeps both sides, a file's items in one of each of its regions, and the generated bindings are regenerated from the merged input. Any other conflict is a defect of the integration, resolved without
   discarding either side. No merge is committed while its tree holds a conflict marker,
   here or wherever a branch takes another by merge, such as a wave's branch taking the
   working branch, so that every branch forked from it starts from a tree that builds.
2. The merge's tree passes the gates of
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section, and in
   a port campaign, in the run that holds the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port`
   items, the module's switch from C to Rust, which happens once, as
   [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes:
   its export feature is deleted, and the C test cases none of its `unit_pub` tests carries
   over are listed before its C tests leave.
3. The working branch is fast-forwarded to the module's branch.

Modules integrate one at a time, and nothing else is committed on the working branch while
one does, so that its fast-forward cannot be rejected. A port's later-stage waves come after
their module's switch, are promoted to the working branch, and integrate nothing, as
the porting workflow's Later stages section describes.

## 5. Lifecycle

Each branch and worktree exists only while its part of the campaign needs it. Before a part starts, everything it is named for exists; once it is promoted, what
## 6. Identity

Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed
as Crustify, whose GitHub account is `crustify-ai` and whose git identity is
`crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>`, whatever the repository's git configuration says,
unless the settings' `identity` answer names another: an author and any co-authors, each
as `Name <email>`. The author named there then authors and commits every commit, and each
message ends with one `Co-Authored-By:` trailer per co-author and no other, none that an
agent's host suggests included.

The identity is passed explicitly, as configuration on the command line, to every command
that writes a commit, a rebase, a merge and a cherry-pick as much as a commit, since the
host may have no git identity of its own.

http.c: switch from C to Rust (modules/libgit2/deps/llhttp/http.c/integration/run-1)

deps/llhttp/http.c is the fourth module to switch, and llhttp's second:
its export feature, ffi-export-deps-llhttp-http-c, is deleted, so that
http.rs's gateway, with its four unit_priv tests, compiles from now on,
and the fork's main drops the TU (c/ at 230c9dbdb, `integrate
deps/llhttp/http.c`). llhttp.c's generated parser reaches the three
hooks, llhttp__before_headers_complete, llhttp__after_headers_complete
and llhttp__after_message_complete, and libgit2's HTTP client
(httpparser.h's git_http_parser_keep_alive, which httpclient.c expands)
llhttp_should_keep_alive, through the exports, in the crate's static
library the C already links (LIBGIT2_RUST_LIBRARY). llhttp.h stays, for
llhttp.c and the HTTP client. headers_code loses its dead_code
expectation, which named the feature: the gateway now uses it always.

The module's six equivalence tests, which need the C, are retired
(tests/equiv/deps/llhttp/http.rs and its mod line), each mapped to the
unit tests that keep its behaviour by the module pass (wave-197/batch-1's
equiv-retirement.md). Every one of them calls C, http.c's own or
llhttp.c's parse, and carries the Miri `calls C` marker, so none is
carried over. The raw binding of llhttp_should_keep_alive stays and
reaches its export; that of llhttp_message_needs_eof, which has no
export and which only http.c's C and its equivalence tests called, goes
with its allowlist entry. The hooks have no header declaration and no
raw binding.

compare the Rust with itself, are retired: the gateway's equiv_priv

equivalence tests stay: the header keeps their C for the remaining C.

regenerated from the new header, they lose their six

The allowlist is unchanged.

# A header module's `static inline` functions are exported, under a feature named for its header

Status: `open`.

Goal: Consistency. A `static inline` function of a header module is one kind of item with
any other module's, and both take one pattern, an export the remaining C calls after the
switch. Interoperability: the C that stays reaches the module through the boundary.
Fitness: the conventions findings reviews file, per item (Consistency's measure), here six
items of one module.

## Signal

Review findings, and an agent prompt that led its agent wrong. `wave-223/batch-1`, the
module pass of the header module `src/util/integer.h`, filed
`conventions/static-inline-functions-without-exports`. `wave-223/batch-0` ported the header's
six `static inline` functions with no export and no gateway, though C in 19 files calls
them. Its docs cite "porting's Macros and Static inline functions sections" as keeping the
header's items in the header.

## Evidence

- The batch's task message, written for the campaign's first header module with `static
  inline` functions, said "An item the remaining C still expands from the header needs no
  export". The batch read "expands" as covering the functions' bodies, which every caller
  inlines, as well as the macros.
- `porting-symbols`' Static inline functions section says what the switch does with such a
  function: "the header's definition is replaced by its prototype, and the remaining C calls
  the Rust module's export". It does not say that this holds where the module is the header
  alone and the header stays. The Macros section, the one the batch followed, says that a
  header macro "stays in its header for the remaining C, unexported". A header module holds
  both kinds, and the two sections read as one rule.
- The conventions' Export features section names a module's feature `ffi-export-<tu>`,
  "with `<tu>` its translation unit's path below the C root". A header module's
  `translation_unit` is `null` (`modules-schema`), so it has no name to give its feature.
  The review named it for the header, `ffi-export-src-util-integer-h`.
- Earlier header modules (`src/util/strnlen.h`, `deps/ntlmclient/compat.h`) held macros
  alone on this build, so none had met the case.

## Destination

The spec: `porting-symbols`' Static inline functions section, and the conventions' Export
features section.

## Change

In `porting-symbols`' Static inline functions section, after its second sentence, add:

> This holds for a header module too, the header alone, which stays while the remaining C
> includes it: its macros stay in it unexported, as Macros describes, and its `static
> inline` functions are exported, their definitions replaced by prototypes at the switch.

In the conventions' Export features section, after its first sentence, add:

> A header module, which has no translation unit, takes its header's path in its place.

## Validation

Not yet validated. The rerun is the item that exposed it, `wave-223/batch-0`'s six
`fn::git__is_*`, under the change and the same task message. It is expected to write the
gateway under `ffi-export-src-util-integer-h` and to document the header's prototypes, as

content.content:
## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as its
`PROPOSAL.md`. It states:

- the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it cites;
- the goal it serves, by name, and the fitness measure of that goal it expects to move;
- its destination;
- the change, or the patch;
- how it was validated;
- the row the record takes when the change lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes;
- its review's verdict; and
- its status: `open`; `deferred`, with what it waits for; `landed`, with the commit it
  landed as; `declined`, with why; or `superseded`, with the proposal that replaces it.

The campaign keeps an index of its proposals, `crustify/evolution/INDEX.md`, one row per
proposal: its slug, its signal in a line, its status, the runs that met the signal, and the
row of the record it matches, if any. The index has one writer per campaign, so that two
runs never write a row at once. It is written as each batch's proposals land, and holds
every proposal of the campaign before a wave launches.

A signal is filed once while its proposal waits. Before a run files a proposal, it reads the
index, in its worktree, and the record, in Crustify's checkout. Campaigns that share a
component's working branch, as a side campaign does with its parent, read each other's index
too:

- where the index holds its signal in a proposal that is `open` or `deferred`, the run files
  nothing new. When that proposal is in the run's own repository, the run adds its evidence
  to it, as an occurrence; otherwise, the run reports the occurrence in its final message,
  and the index's writer records it;
- otherwise, where its signal meets the recurrence signal of a row of the record, the change
  that landed did not hold: the run files a new proposal that cites the row, as
  [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s Record section describes; and
- otherwise, the run files the proposal.

A lesson is not filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it. A defect in a tool found
while reviewing is a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed code, and is filed with its
reproducer.

## 5. Lessons

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
before its first step. Each lesson is one entry, under a heading that is its id: a short
slug no other lesson of the file has. An entry holds a status, one rule, the evidence the
rule rests on, and, on a line of its own, its scope: the modules, items or stages it holds
for.

A lesson steers every later run, as a rule of the spec does, so it is reviewed:

- A new or changed lesson is `provisional`. The first review batch whose worklist holds the
  commit that added or changed it reads it, against its evidence, its scope and the
  generality test of [Destinations](#3-destinations). A lesson no worklist holds, such as
  one a wave's last review batch adds, is read by the next review batch the campaign
  launches.
- The review batch that reads a lesson marks it `held` in its landing. A lesson it judges
  wrong, or one that belongs in the spec, is a finding of that batch: under `fix`, the
  batch corrects the entry, retires it, or files the proposal it should have been.
- A lesson the code no longer supports is `retired`. It stays in the file, marked, with
  why.
- An edit changes one entry. The file is never rewritten whole, since a rewrite drops what
  its writer did not think to keep.

The lessons are reconciled at each ship point, and whenever five have been added or changed
since the last pass: duplicates are merged, stale lessons are retired, scopes are checked,
and a lesson that can be stated without the target's names is proposed for the spec, as is
one a second campaign records again, by a proposal citing both. A lesson the pass changes
is `provisional` again.

## 6. Changes

A campaign evolves each component, Crustify or a tool, on a working branch of its own in
that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.

A change is made on a branch named `<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>`, forked from that
working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a
fast-forward, the worktree is purged and the branch deleted. Its commits take the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
campaign's.

- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
  as generally as the evidence allows.
- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect
  becomes one, and a new behaviour gets one that fails without it. A change to its
  documentation alone adds none, unless the defect it fixes has a reproducer, which becomes
  a test or a doctest. A packaging defect's reproducer becomes a test too, run
  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.
- A new tool is drafted and tested where it serves a repeated procedure, preferably as a
  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
  merged upstream only with the user's approval.

A fix that unblocks the campaign, or that would prevent a defect in later campaigns, is
landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.

## 7. Validation

content.content:
## 7. Validation

A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.

A spec change that a failure prompted is validated by running again what failed, the item,
the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.

A rerun shows that a change answers the case that exposed it, not that it holds: that is
watched in the campaigns after it lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes.

## 8. Review

Every change is reviewed before it lands, on its evolution branch, by a run other than the
one that made it. A change is finished once its proposal names its commit. A finished
change is reviewed before the next wave of its campaign launches, so that later runs work on
the fix rather than around it. The review reads the proposal, the change and its validation, and checks
that:

- the proposal's evidence shows the signal, and the change answers it;
- the change serves a goal, and a tool's stays within the tool's own goals;
- it is placed and written as [`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md) describes, and states
  no rule in the target's names;
- its validation was run, and shows what the proposal says;
- the row its proposal drafts for the record, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes, names a recurrence
  signal a campaign would observe, and `test` only where its test checks all of it; and
- whether it weakens a check, which the verdict marks.

A review runs under the campaign's working branch of the component, never under the change
it reviews, and reads the change from its branch. Its task pins the commit it reviews, and
only that commit lands, by a fast-forward of the working branch: a commit added after the
verdict, or one a rebase or cherry-pick makes, is reviewed again. A rebase of a change to
the text of skills, agents or templates alone, no script or program among its files, is the
exception, where each file the commit changes is the same in the rebased commit and its
parent as in the reviewed commit and its parent: the review then read the same diff against
the same text. Its checks are this section's and its
role's; the task message of the run that asks for it adds to them, and never relaxes them.
A review reads as deeply as the change reaches: a change to documentation alone is read; a
tool's code, a check, a soundness fix and every rule of the spec are reviewed with their
validation run again.

The verdict is recorded in the proposal's Review section, approved or rejected, with its
reasons; a rejection leaves the proposal open for another change or for the user.

What only records what was decided changes no rule and is not reviewed: a row of the index,
a status of the record, or a proposal's status, verdict and review. A row of the record is
reviewed in its proposal, with its change.

A change that weakens a check, a gate, a test, a lint, a review objective, a tool's
detection or a rule of this skill, is marked so in the verdict and in its entry of the
record, since a run that can loosen what judges it passes by loosening it: the user reads
each such change on its own before `devel` takes it, as [Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

## 9. Autonomy

The settings' `evolution` answer sets how far a campaign evolves the harness:

| answer | what lands on the campaign's working branches |
|---|---|
| `off` | nothing: no proposal, no lesson |
| `propose` | nothing but the index's rows and the record's statuses: proposals and lessons are filed, and no rule changes |
| `repair` | each fix of a defect |
| `evolve` | also each improvement and discovery |

A change lands on its component's working branch as soon as its review approves it, without
the user's approval: the working branch is the campaign's own, and nothing else runs on it.

The protected paths are the exception. They hold what judges the work, and a run that can
loosen what judges it passes by loosening it. In Crustify's repository they are:

- `GOALS.md`;
- `skills/crustify/evolution/**` and `skills/verification/**`, the scripts beside those
  skills included;
- `skills/artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md`;
- the Lints and Unsafe code sections of `skills/rust/toolchain/SKILL.md`;
- the Testing, Reviewing and Audit sections of `skills/tools/*/SKILL.md`, and every section
  of one that describes a scan a landing passes, such as `ffimap`'s Binding › Safe boundary;
- `agents/common.md`, `agents/reviewer.md` and the Evolution section of
  `agents/assistant/assistant.md`;
- the `evolution` question of `templates/*/CRUSTIFY.template.md`;
- `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, which decides the skills and hooks a run loads; and
- `providers/generic/compose.py` and, under `providers/claude/`, `compose.py`, `spawn.py`,
  `system-prompt.md`, `hooks.json` and `agents/*.md`. A generated agent that changes only as
  its sources outside this list changed is not a change to a protected path.

A change whose diff touches a protected path lands on the working branch only with the
user's approval, whatever its review says, and so does the removal of a `weakens a check`
mark from the record. One case lands without that approval: the repair of a defect in
protected code, a script or a provider's program, that blocks the campaign, once its review
approves it and finds three things. The repair weakens no check. Every existing test of the
code it touches is unchanged. The repair adds a regression test of its own. Such a repair is
put to the user at the next module's end. A change to a protected text always waits for the
user. A
change to `GOALS.md` is proposed and never made, unless the user asks for it, since
`GOALS.md` is what every other change is judged against.

A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.

A run that a defect blocks does not work around it. Where the answer lets fixes land, it
makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
batch is.

## 10. Adoption

Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it

the text of skills, agents or templates alone, no script or program among its files, is the
exception, where each file the commit changes is the same in the rebased commit and its
parent as in the reviewed commit and its parent: the review then read the same diff against
the same text. Its checks are this section's and its
role's; the task message of the run that asks for it adds to them, and never relaxes them.
A review reads as deeply as the change reaches: a change to documentation alone is read; a
tool's code, a check, a soundness fix and every rule of the spec are reviewed with their
validation run again.

The verdict is recorded in the proposal's Review section, approved or rejected, with its
reasons; a rejection leaves the proposal open for another change or for the user.

What only records what was decided changes no rule and is not reviewed: a row of the index,
a status of the record, or a proposal's status, verdict and review. A row of the record is
reviewed in its proposal, with its change.

A change that weakens a check, a gate, a test, a lint, a review objective, a tool's
detection or a rule of this skill, is marked so in the verdict and in its entry of the
record, since a run that can loosen what judges it passes by loosening it: the user reads
each such change on its own before `devel` takes it, as [Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

## 9. Autonomy

The settings' `evolution` answer sets how far a campaign evolves the harness:

| answer | what lands on the campaign's working branches |
|---|---|
| `off` | nothing: no proposal, no lesson |
| `propose` | nothing but the index's rows and the record's statuses: proposals and lessons are filed, and no rule changes |
| `repair` | each fix of a defect |
| `evolve` | also each improvement and discovery |

A change lands on its component's working branch as soon as its review approves it, without
the user's approval: the working branch is the campaign's own, and nothing else runs on it.

The protected paths are the exception. They hold what judges the work, and a run that can
loosen what judges it passes by loosening it. In Crustify's repository they are:

- `GOALS.md`;
- `skills/crustify/evolution/**` and `skills/verification/**`, the scripts beside those
  skills included;
- `skills/artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md`;
- the Lints and Unsafe code sections of `skills/rust/toolchain/SKILL.md`;
- the Testing, Reviewing and Audit sections of `skills/tools/*/SKILL.md`, and every section
  of one that describes a scan a landing passes, such as `ffimap`'s Binding › Safe boundary;
- `agents/common.md`, `agents/reviewer.md` and the Evolution section of
  `agents/assistant/assistant.md`;
- the `evolution` question of `templates/*/CRUSTIFY.template.md`;
- `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, which decides the skills and hooks a run loads; and
- `providers/generic/compose.py` and, under `providers/claude/`, `compose.py`, `spawn.py`,
  `system-prompt.md`, `hooks.json` and `agents/*.md`. A generated agent that changes only as
  its sources outside this list changed is not a change to a protected path.

A change whose diff touches a protected path lands on the working branch only with the
user's approval, whatever its review says, and so does the removal of a `weakens a check`
mark from the record. One case lands without that approval: the repair of a defect in
protected code, a script or a provider's program, that blocks the campaign, once its review
approves it and finds three things. The repair weakens no check. Every existing test of the
code it touches is unchanged. The repair adds a regression test of its own. Such a repair is
put to the user at the next module's end. A change to a protected text always waits for the
user. A
change to `GOALS.md` is proposed and never made, unless the user asks for it, since
`GOALS.md` is what every other change is judged against.

A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.

A run that a defect blocks does not work around it. Where the answer lets fixes land, it
makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
batch is.

## 10. Adoption

Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it

# A switch's Rust side lands before its builds, and removes every mention of the export feature

Status: `landed` as crustify `10500c9` (record `91ea0cc`) on `libgit2-crustify/devel`, on 2026-11-14: the
approved `d3e56f0` rebased, its file the same in the commit and its parent. Split from
`module-switch-procedure` that day.

Goal: Incremental migration without breaking consumers. Its measure counts the landed trees
that failed a gate.

## Signal

"Skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong": a defect
in the spec. `porting-workflow`'s Builds section lists a switch's steps in an order that
cannot be run (item 10), and its words "its export feature is deleted" read as fewer edits
than the lints need (item 14).

## Evidence

**The switch's Rust side precedes the generation (item 10).** Met at the third switch,
`deps/llhttp/api.c`'s (`modules/libgit2/deps/llhttp/api.c/integration/run-1`, the fork's
`c54c0c180`, dashboard Notes entry `libgit2/deps/llhttp/api.c` integration). It is the first
switch that removes raw bindings: 23 functions without an export, with their allowlist
entries. Each variant's `build` runs `rust-staticlib.sh`, which builds the crate of the
checkout with `--features bindgen` in campaign mode, checking the committed bindings against
the variant's headers, and compiles the gateway only once the export feature is gone. So the
switch's Rust side, the feature deleted, the allowlist pruned and the bindings regenerated,
comes before `build-variants.sh`, not after the C's removal as the procedure's order (the C
change, then the variants, then the gates) suggests. The bindings are regenerated against
the previous generation, whose headers the switch does not change.

- The run deleted the feature, pruned `sys/libgit2/allowlist.txt` of the 23 functions and
  regenerated `bindings.rs` (`CRUSTIFY_BINDINGS_UPDATE=1 cargo-variant.sh plain build
  --features bindgen --lib`, against gen2), committed that, and only then committed the C
  change and ran `build-variants.sh`, whose `rust-staticlib.sh` then checked the committed
  bindings against gen3's headers on every variant.
- Item 10 again, at `deps/llhttp/http.c`'s switch
  (`modules/libgit2/deps/llhttp/http.c/integration/run-1`, the fork's `230c9dbdb`): the run
  deleted the feature, pruned the allowlist of `llhttp_message_needs_eof` and regenerated
  `bindings.rs` against gen4, committed that with the submodule at the fork's new commit, and
  only then ran `build-variants.sh`.

**The export feature is named outside the gateway's `cfg` (item 14).** Met at the fourth
switch, `deps/llhttp/http.c`'s. The switch deletes "the module's export feature", which
reads as the `Cargo.toml` entry and the gateway's `#[cfg(feature = …)]`. http.c's
`headers_code`, which only the gateway calls, also carried
`#[cfg_attr(not(any(test, feature = "ffi-export-deps-llhttp-http-c")), expect(dead_code))]`:
with the feature gone, the unknown `cfg` and the expectation left unmet fail clippy with
warnings denied. The module pass foresaw it, so the switch did not fail; nothing in the
procedure would have. The step is mechanical: every mention of the feature's name in the
crate (`src/`, `tests/`, `Cargo.toml`, `build.rs`) is removed or rewritten, a `cfg_attr` or
`cfg(any(…))` that names it as much as the gateway's attribute, so that only the run records
and the reviews' reproducers (item 7) still name it.

- `grep -rn ffi-export-deps-llhttp-http-c` over `src`, `tests`, `Cargo.toml` and `build.rs`
  found the `Cargo.toml` entry, the gateway's `cfg`, `headers_code`'s `cfg_attr` and the
  module's doc comment; after the switch it finds none there.

**The order within one variant's build (from item 2's evidence).** At the first switch
(`modules/libgit2/src/util/utf8.c/integration/run-1`, commits `012d1d34c` and the fork's
`1b37e3d08`), `crustify/scripts/rust-staticlib.sh` runs as the first step of each variant's
`build`, between `configure` and `cmake --build`: the Rust library needs the files
`configure` writes, and the C's link needs the Rust library.

## Destination

From the original's Destination list:

- `porting-workflow`, Builds: the order a switch's steps take, the C build's `configure`
  before the Rust library and its link after it.
- `porting-workflow`, Builds (item 10): the switch's Rust side, the bindings regenerated,
  lands before the generation is built, since every variant's build checks them.
- `porting-workflow`, Builds (item 14): deleting the export feature removes every mention of
  its name in the crate, not only the gateway's `cfg`.

Protected: none. `porting-workflow` (`skills/workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md`) is not
protected.

`testing-gates`' Regressions section, which is protected, repeats the steps in one sentence
("removes its translation unit …, rebuilds the variants from the C that remains and deletes
the module's export feature"). The original does not name it for these items. If its order
is read as binding, it would follow.

## Change

Made, in `porting-workflow`'s Builds section, as an ordered list of the step's four parts after
the paragraph that describes the switch. The sentence "The shared variants are rebuilt from the
C that remains once the integration lands" is removed: the list's third part states the
builds, and `setup`'s and `testing-builds`' Builds sections already say the shared variants are
rebuilt after a landing that changes the compiled target. What was
drafted first:

`porting-workflow`'s Builds section would state a switch's steps in the order they run:

1. The Rust side first, as one commit. The module's export feature is deleted. The allowlist
   entries of the module's functions and globals that have no export are removed. The
   bindings are regenerated against the builds in use, whose headers the switch does not
   change.
2. Deleting the export feature removes or rewrites every mention of its name in the crate:
   its sources, its tests, its manifest and its build script. A `cfg_attr` or a
   `cfg(any(…))` that names the feature counts as much as the gateway's attribute. After
   the step, only run records and review reproducers still name it. The reason is that an
   unknown `cfg`, or a lint expectation left unmet, fails the lints with warnings denied.
3. The C side next: the module's translation unit and its tied C tests leave the fork, and
   the campaign's commit records the submodule at the fork's new commit.
4. The builds last. Each variant is configured, then the Rust library is built, then the C
   is built and linked. The reason is that each variant's build checks the committed
   bindings against its headers, so the bindings must be committed first.
5. The gates run over the new builds.

No script moves with this proposal.

## Record

The row for `EVOLUTION.md`, copied in when the change lands:

| change | from | landed as | signal answered | recurrence signal | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| a switch's Rust side and C side both come before its builds, and the gates after, and deleting the export feature removes every mention of its name in the crate | `libgit2-crustify`, `switch-step-order` | crustify `10500c9` | `porting-workflow` had the variants rebuilt once the integration lands, though the remaining C links exports the Rust library holds only once the feature is deleted, and "the export feature is deleted" read as fewer edits than the lints need | an integration run whose builds precede its Rust side, or whose lints fail on a mention of a deleted export feature | watched |

## Validation

# When a ported `static inline` function stays in its header

Status: `open`.

## Signal

Two texts disagree, and a run had to follow one of them against the other (`evolution` §2,
"skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong").
`porting-symbols` § Static inline functions has every ported `static inline` function lose its
header definition at its module's switch: "the header's definition is replaced by its
prototype, and the remaining C calls the Rust module's export". `porting-workflow` § 1.1 states
the principle behind it: "each function has one implementation". The task message of
`wave-226/batch-1/run-1` said the opposite, and cited `porting-symbols` for it: "A macro or a
`static inline` function the remaining C expands from `thread.h` or `unix/pthread.h` stays in
the header and needs no export, as `porting-symbols` describes". The section says that of a
header's macros, not of its `static inline` functions.

## Evidence

`wave-226/batch-1/run-1` (`src/util/thread.c`, symbol route) ports `thread.h`'s eleven
`static inline` atomic operations, `git_atomic32_{get,set,inc,dec,add}`,
`git_atomic64_{get,set,add}` and `git_atomic__{compare_and_swap,swap,load}`. Each body is one
`__atomic` builtin in this build: no call, no state of the module. wavefront lists 57 C
callers of `git_atomic32_inc` alone: every `GIT_REFCOUNT_INC`, the runtime's `init_count`, and
the object cache's total. None of them is ported. The run followed the task message. The ports
are native methods (`Atomic32Ref::inc` and its siblings, `atomic_compare_and_swap` over a
pointer-sized standard atomic). There is no export and no export feature, and `thread.h`
keeps its bodies.

The two forms are equivalent where C and Rust share an object. Both are the C11 memory model's
sequentially consistent operations on the same bytes. The run's equivalence tests run C's
`git_atomic32_inc` and the port's from four threads on one count, and race C's and Rust's
compare-and-swap on one slot. Both pass, plain, under ASan+UBSan and under TSan.

Under the section as written, the same port would make these changes at the switch:

- replace each body by a prototype;
- route every reference count's increment in the remaining C through an exported Rust call
  that cannot be inlined, since cross-language LTO is the section's own TODO; and
- add eleven exports and their gateway.

These changes keep no behaviour the header does not already keep. They also change no state
the Rust holds: the C's body reaches nothing of the module but the object it is given. The
same holds for any C function whose body is the language's own operations on its arguments:
an atomic builtin, a byte swap, an arithmetic helper.

## Goal

Correctness of the spec (no two texts disagree), and Idiomatic Rust / performance: what C
expands keeps its native code. The fitness measure: no task message contradicts
`porting-symbols`, and no export is added that only forwards one builtin.

## Destination

The spec: `porting-symbols` § Static inline functions. It is unprotected, and the translator
role evolves it.

## Change

Add a paragraph to `porting-symbols` § 4, after its first:

> A `static inline` function whose body reaches nothing but its arguments and the operations
> of the language and its compiler, such as an atomic builtin or a byte swap, keeps its body
> in its header for the remaining C, as a header's macro does. It is unexported, and its C and
> Rust forms are not linked beyond the Rust form's annotation. They share no state, so the
> one implementation `porting-workflow`'s Principles section asks for is the Rust one for
> Rust consumers. A remaining C caller that expands the header keeps the header's
> instructions, which an export it could not inline would only slow. Its equivalence tests
> compare the two forms. Where C and Rust share an object it works on, they also run both
> forms on it at once. The body goes when its header goes, with the last C file that
> includes it.

`porting-workflow` § 1.3's sentence on the headers bundled with a module, "declaring the
module's exports, its `static inline` functions included", gains "but those `porting-symbols`
leaves defined in them".

## Validation

None run: the rule is the one `wave-226/batch-1/run-1` followed under its task message. A
rerun under the change would produce the same port, so the change only removes the
contradiction. Whether a body "reaches nothing but its arguments" is read from the source, as
the analysis reads it now.

input.content:
# A switch whose C side changes a header makes it before the bindings are regenerated

Status: `open`.

Goal: Incremental migration without breaking consumers. Its measure counts the landed trees
that failed a gate.

## Signal

"Skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong": a defect
in the spec. `porting-workflow`'s Builds section orders a switch's parts as the Rust side,
"the bindings … regenerated against the builds in use, whose headers the switch does not
change", then the C side. `bindgen`'s Generation section has the bindings follow "from the
headers at the `c/` revision", their source dirs "taken from the checkout's `c/`". A switch
whose C side changes a header the bindings read, as a `static inline` function's switch
does when it replaces the definition by its prototype (`porting-symbols`' Static inline
functions section), therefore changes the bindings by its C side: in the order the section
gives, the Rust side's regeneration reads the header unchanged and changes nothing, and
every variant's build of the new generation, which checks the committed bindings against
the checkout's headers, fails.

## Evidence

`src/util/integer.h`'s switch (`modules/libgit2/src/util/integer.h/integration/run-1`, the
campaign's fifth and its first of a header module, commit `b95941fa6` and the fork's
`d9a1d699b`). The header's six `GIT_INLINE` functions were bound through `static_fns.c`'s
wrappers, `git__is_<name>__extern`, and their raw bindings carried
`#[link_name = "git__is_<name>__extern"]`. The switch replaces the six definitions by
prototypes, so that the remaining C calls the module's exports.

- The run made the C side first: `c/src/util/integer.h` changed and committed on the fork's
  `fork/main` as `integrate src/util/integer.h`. Only then did
  `CRUSTIFY_BINDINGS_UPDATE=1 crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh plain build --features
  bindgen --lib`, against gen5 (the builds in use, whose generated headers the switch does
  not change), regenerate the bindings: `bindings.rs` lost the six `link_name` lines and
  `static_fns.c` its six wrappers. The Rust side's one commit records the submodule at
  `d9a1d699b` beside them.
- The module pass's rehearsal on `plain` (`wave-223/batch-1/run-1`'s
  `switch-rehearsal.md`) found the same diff only from a tree whose header was already
  changed.
- The earlier switches removed whole translation units, whose headers stayed as they were,
  so the order held for them: `deps/llhttp/api.c`'s and `deps/llhttp/http.c`'s
  regenerated against the previous generation after pruning the allowlist, as
  `switch-step-order` records.

The record's row of `switch-step-order` watches "an integration run whose builds precede its
Rust side, or whose lints fail on a mention of a deleted export feature": this is neither,
so the proposal is new.

## Destination

The spec: `porting-workflow`'s Builds section, the first two parts of a switch.

Protected: none. `porting-workflow` (`skills/workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md`) is not
protected.

## Change

In `porting-workflow`'s Builds section, the end of part 1, "and the bindings are regenerated
against the builds in use, whose headers the switch does not change.", becomes:

> and the bindings are regenerated against the builds in use, whose generated headers the
> switch does not change. The bindings follow from the checkout's `c/` headers, as
> [`bindgen`](../../rust/bindgen/SKILL.md)'s Generation section describes: where the C side
> changes a header they read, such as a `static inline` definition replaced by its
> prototype, the C side is committed on the fork first, and the regeneration and the
> submodule's new commit land in this commit.

Made on `libgit2-crustify/evolution/switch-header-change-before-bindings` of Crustify, in
`skills/workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md` alone.

## Validation

The failure the change answers was not run as such: this switch followed the changed order
from the start, from the rehearsal's finding. What it produced under the changed order is
the evidence above: the regenerated bindings match the rehearsal's diff exactly, and
`build-variants.sh` built gen6's five variants from `d9a1d699b`, each variant's
`rust-staticlib.sh` checking the committed bindings against the checkout's headers with no
difference. The rerun the review may ask for is a scratch copy of `12dfd634d` with the
feature deleted, regenerated before the header changes (no diff expected), then
`rust-staticlib.sh plain` in a build configured from `d9a1d699b` (a bindings mismatch
expected).

## Record

The row for `EVOLUTION.md`, copied in when the change lands:

| change | from | landed as | signal answered | recurrence signal | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| a switch whose C side changes a header the bindings read commits that C side before regenerating them, in the Rust side's one commit | `libgit2-crustify`, `switch-header-change-before-bindings` | crustify (its commit) | `porting-workflow` regenerated a switch's bindings before its C side, so a header the switch changes left them stale and every variant's bindings check failed | a switch whose committed bindings differ from those its new generation's builds regenerate, or a variant build failing the bindings check after a switch | watched |

## Review

Pending.

s=open(p).read()
old="""   functions and globals that have no export are removed, and the bindings are regenerated

"""
new="""   functions and globals that have no export are removed, and the bindings are regenerated
   against the builds in use, whose generated headers the switch does not change. The
   bindings follow from the checkout's `c/` headers, as
   [`bindgen`](../../rust/bindgen/SKILL.md)'s Generation section describes: where the C side
   changes a header they read, such as a `static inline` definition replaced by its
   prototype, the C side is committed on the fork first, and the regeneration and the
   submodule's new commit land in this commit.
"""
assert s.count(old)==1
open(p,'w').write(s.replace(old,new))
EOF
git diff --stat; git add -A && git -c user.name='Marius Momeu' -c user.email='marius.momeu@berkeley.edu' commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
porting-workflow: a switch's header change precedes its bindings

A switch whose C side changes a header the raw bindings read, as a
static inline function's prototype does, commits that C side on the fork
before the Rust side regenerates the bindings, which follow from the
checkout's c/ headers; the regeneration and the submodule's new commit
land in the Rust side's one commit. Met at libgit2-crustify's
src/util/integer.h switch (modules/libgit2/src/util/integer.h/integration/run-1);
proposal switch-header-change-before-bindings.

Co-Authored-By: crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>
EOF
git log --oneline -1
